content.title: About
content.content: Duck eggs are larger than chicken eggs, with a thicker smooth shell that is white, pale blue, or greenish. They have a large, rich yolk and a firm white, and the taste is richer and fattier than chicken eggs. Duck eggs are boiled, fried, used in baking, and made into preserved and salted eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A duck egg is noticeably larger and heavier than a chicken egg.
The shell of a duck egg is thicker and tougher than that of a chicken egg.
In Asia, duck eggs are salted and cured, and are also made into century eggs.
In Southeast Asia, people eat balut, a special dish made from a fertilized duck egg.
Thanks to the fatty yolk, duck eggs are valued in baking: baked goods come out more tender and rich.

items.title: Source of complete protein
items.content: The egg provides protein with all the essential amino acids.

items.title: Contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin
items.content: These vitamins support metabolism and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contain iron and selenium
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport, and selenium is a trace mineral with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contain choline
items.content: Choline is important for nervous system function and cell membranes.

items.title: Contain vitamins A and D
items.content: The yolk contains the fat-soluble vitamins A and D.

items.title: Salmonella
items.content: Duck eggs may contain Salmonella, so they should be boiled or fried until the white and yolk are firm; this is especially important for children, pregnant women, older adults, and people with weakened immunity.

items.title: Cholesterol and fat
items.content: A duck egg has more fat and cholesterol than a chicken egg; people with high cholesterol should discuss how many to eat with a doctor.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: One egg is higher in calories than a chicken egg, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Egg allergy is possible, including cross-reaction with chicken eggs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hard-boil duck eggs for about 10–12 minutes, fry them, make omelets, and add them to dough, pasta, and desserts. Eat them only fully cooked, with a firm white and yolk. In baking, one duck egg can roughly replace one to two chicken eggs, following the recipe.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator in their package, away from strong-smelling foods, and use them before the expiration date. Do not wash them in advance. Keep boiled eggs in the refrigerator for a few days. Discard cracked eggs and eggs with an unpleasant smell.
